look_here_first: TEXAS BROME: native Texas annual with soft hairy sheaths/nodes, open panicle and 4–7-flowered narrow awned spikelets. SOURCE-IDENTIFIED flowering photo (gallery 0) shows actual yellow anthers and spikelets; it does NOT prove roots or collar. Before confusing with introduced Japanese/lanceolate or other Bromus, dissect mature LOWER 1-veined + UPPER 3-veined glumes and check lemma/awn, ligule, growth form and verified source. WARNING: the 1/3 glume pattern alone is NOT unique to this species (e.g., downy brome also shares it). Do not authorize removal based on flowerhead silhouette or one vein pair alone.

curation_status.visual_finish: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — nine exact-species Texas real photos plus historical illustration, including live rocky-slope growth, sheath, true culm node, open inner collar membrane, awned spikelets. Exposed connected fibrous crown, measured intact 1–3 mm ligule, separated 1-/3-veined glumes and independently measured mature lemma apex still missing.

learner_visual_status.note: Nine physically stored genuine research-grade Texas brome JPEGs from two CC BY photographers/three observations, plus a separate historical PD drawing. Fifteen gallery panels include nine own-species photographs, one illustration and five look-alikes; contact-sheet checked true opened collar tissue, node and in-situ plant. No root extraction, 1mm certified ligule or glume/lemma dissection. No live Pages/mobile QA verified.

best_field_traits: NATIVE TEXAS BROME: prioritize the GLUME VEIN KEY before invasive control. On a mature intact spikelet, lower glume usually ONE vein (~6–9 mm) and upper THREE (~8–10.5 mm); FNA describes ~20–30 mm spikelet, 4–7 florets, ~9–15 mm lemma and 4–8 mm awn. Japanese brome often has 3–5 lower and ~7 upper glume veins. Mere YELLOW ANTHERS, hairy sheaths or hanging heads do NOT prove native versus introduced.
GENUS: Bromus PANICLES carry MULTI-FLOWERED spikelets; outer pair = GLUMES, inner overlapping units = LEMMAS, often with AWNS; not a true Hordeum/Elymus rachis SPIKE.
Annual Texas native; keep state-scale status separate from county-voucher science review.
An open, often few-spikeleted panicle of elongated green, later straw, awned multi-flowered spikelets.
Kew typical mature spikelet ~20 mm with 6–8 florets; historic Texas treatment gives 20–30 mm with 4–7 florets; don't overfit one number.
Fertile lemma about 9–12 mm, awn ~6–10 mm in GrassBase; mature lower glume commonly ONE vein, upper THREE veins.
Rescuegrass B. catharticus is COMPARISON ONLY: large BROAD FLATTENED spikelets with short or no awns; many awned bromes differ from it.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Fresh whole plant plus annual crown and habitat
Two mature spikelets with actual mm ruler
Mature lemma apex and straight 4–8 mm awn, showing insertion below an entire acute/subulate tip (FNA); record alternate descriptions without assuming visible teeth
Hairy sheath and real ligule collar
crew_field_check: LOOK AT THE SPIKELET, NOT JUST THE DROOP: all four bromes have several florets stacked along one spikelet, often with lemma awns. First decide ANNUAL vs PERENNIAL, then count florets, measure the entire spikelet, individual lemma and awn, and inspect the glume veins and leaf sheath hairs. Nodding inflorescences or long awns alone are not a species ID.
Measure actual mature spikelet(s) with a millimeter ruler.
Inspect lemma/glume or true ligule ONLY where detailed pixels or a collected macro are actually available.
Record uncertain grass to genus, don't force the species from one photo.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Japanese brome — Bromus japonicus: Introduced cool-season annual. Usually small-to-moderate narrow awned spikelets on flexible, often nodding/kinked panicle branches. Flora of North America typically gives lower glume 3–5 veins, upper 7 veins; separate from native Texas brome's 1/3-veined pair. Lanceolate brome — Bromus lanceolatus: Introduced annual. Typically larger long lance-shaped spikelets ~25–50 mm, with roughly 8–20 florets and ~12–18 mm mature lemmas; open panicle. Hairy woodland brome — Bromus pubescens: Native North American woodland perennial, often taller with broader soft leaves, and open drooping panicle. Shorter generally straight lemma awns commonly 3–8 mm. Lower glume typically 1-veined; true pubescence may be obvious on entire lemma. Texas brome — Bromus texensis: Texas-native annual restricted to limited Texas sites. Flora of North America: often 20–30 mm spikelets with 4–7 florets, lower glume ONE vein (~6–9 mm), upper THREE (~8–10.5 mm), lemma ~9–15 mm and awn ~4–8 mm. Rescuegrass — Bromus catharticus (comparison only): Introduced South American cool-season grass, often annual or short-lived perennial depending ecology/treatment. Larger broad 16–40 mm strongly flattened spikelets, many florets and short/no awns (often 0–4 mm).

field_matrix.where_to_look: At flowering inspect loose kinked/arching panicle BRANCHES; at fruit inspect lower/upper glume VEINS on intact source-verified spikelet.
field_matrix.look_alike: Introduced cool-season annual. Usually small-to-moderate narrow awned spikelets on flexible, often nodding/kinked panicle branches. Flora of North America typically gives lower glume 3–5 veins, upper 7 veins; separate from native Texas brome's 1/3-veined pair.
field_matrix.confirmation: Open macro: overlapping lemmas have long often twisted/recurving awns from below their apices; source descriptions vary considerably in spikelet length. Do not use a 10–15 mm cutoff to exclude Japanese brome.
field_matrix.avoid_false_identification: Nodding and awns also occur in native Texas brome; compare intact mature glumes and source-labelled specimen.
field_matrix.quick_rule: Use whole flowering panicle + intact mature multi-flowered spikelet measurements together.

field_matrix.where_to_look: Measure an intact mature spikelet including ALL florets excluding its awns, then count fertile florets.
field_matrix.look_alike: Introduced annual. Typically larger long lance-shaped spikelets ~25–50 mm, with roughly 8–20 florets and ~12–18 mm mature lemmas; open panicle.
field_matrix.confirmation: Compare long often pointed spikelets with Japanese brome's often smaller fewer florets, but both dimensions vary; check true lemma body and awn attachment at 10–20×.
field_matrix.avoid_false_identification: Length alone overlaps rescuegrass and native bromes; always count florets and inspect glumes.
field_matrix.quick_rule: Use whole flowering panicle + intact mature multi-flowered spikelet measurements together.

field_matrix.where_to_look: Look at actual rooted crown, then hairy lemma surface at 10× and sheath/true collar.
field_matrix.look_alike: Native North American woodland perennial, often taller with broader soft leaves, and open drooping panicle. Shorter generally straight lemma awns commonly 3–8 mm. Lower glume typically 1-veined; true pubescence may be obvious on entire lemma.
field_matrix.confirmation: A mature persistent perennial tuft/crown and hairy lemmas support pubescens, unlike short-lived Japanese, lanceolate and Texas annuals.
field_matrix.avoid_false_identification: Hairy sheaths alone are NOT proof: multiple annual bromes have pubescent sheaths too. 389×589 archived source doesn't show lemma hairs.
field_matrix.quick_rule: Use whole flowering panicle + intact mature multi-flowered spikelet measurements together.

field_matrix.where_to_look: Whole flowering panicle: look for big FLAT, broad, oat-like spikelets with very SHORT or absent awns.
field_matrix.look_alike: Introduced South American cool-season grass, often annual or short-lived perennial depending ecology/treatment. Larger broad 16–40 mm strongly flattened spikelets, many florets and short/no awns (often 0–4 mm).
field_matrix.confirmation: Large flattened overlapping V/oat-like florets contrast with Japanese brome's narrow long-awned units and lanceolate brome's narrower long densely floret spikelets.
field_matrix.avoid_false_identification: Not installed in learner. Annual-versus-perennial is NOT sufficient: Texas A&M treats annual, Kew often perennial.
field_matrix.quick_rule: Use whole flowering panicle + intact mature multi-flowered spikelet measurements together.

not_reliable_alone: One awn length, purple seedhead color, or an overall nodding silhouette without attached spikelets.
Soft hair on lower SHEATH: found on multiple introduced and native Bromus species.
Whole head length alone: Flora of North America, Kew GrassBase and Texas regional treatments report overlapping but non-identical ranges.
Lower and upper glume vein count from a photograph that doesn't actually resolve the glumes under backlight.
Presence of yellow extruded ANTHERS: diagnostic of flowering grass stage, NOT Bromus texensis species.
An apparently perennial tuft when broken roots or mowing obscure annual/reproductive life cycle.
Unreviewed county nativity; rare native Texas brome may resemble introduced Japanese brome.

Two visible teeth at the Texas brome lemma tip: FNA describes an entire acute/subulate apex, while some other sources vary; neither description can be judged from the existing photo. Prioritize a mature measured 1/3-veined glume pair.

field_id_finish_pass.crew_teaching_summary: Native Texas annual; inspect mature narrow spikelets with 4–7 florets. Flora of North America describes lemmas 9–15 mm long, an entire acute/subulate apex and a straight 4–8 mm awn inserted just below the tip. Compare mature lower/upper glumes (usually 1 and 3 veins), lemma length and awn with introduced Japanese and lanceolate bromes. Yellow flowering anthers are not species-specific; other treatments differ on tip terminology, so never force this identification from apparent teeth.
field_id_finish_pass.lookalike_comparison: B. japonicus is an introduced annual with slender, flexuous and sometimes nodding panicle branches; reported spikelet size overlaps native B. texensis, so use lower/upper glume nerves (typically 3–5/7 versus 1/3). B. lanceolatus has densely many-flowered longer lanceolate spikelets; B. pubescens is a woodland perennial with hairy lemmas. Green slender spikelets alone are never enough for a native-versus-introduced call.

visual_comparison.title: Texas brome — four installed bromes vs rescuegrass
visual_comparison.subtitle: One locally archived genuine Texas-brome flowering JPEG and one separate public-domain historical multi-taxon botanical plate (ILLUSTRATION, not a specimen photo). Five additional panels belong to different Bromus species: Japanese, lanceolate, woodland and two rescuegrass. None depicts a Texas-brome true ligule, root crown, or separated glumes.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: JAPANESE: annual, flexuous awned head, higher glume veins. TEXAS: annual, lower ONE & upper THREE glume veins. LANCEOLATE: giant many-flowered spikelets. WOODLAND: perennial + hairy lemmas. RESCUE: broad flat short/no-awn units (comparison only).

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Texas brome — one real species photo, verify glumes + ligule before management
steps: 1 · TRUE PHOTO: photo/panel 0 is Cleveland Powell's flowering Bromus texensis source photo with narrow green multi-flowered spikelets and yellow anthers. Roots and true leaf collar are OFF FRAME.
2 · NOT PHOTOGRAPHIC EVIDENCE: panel 1 is a historically public-domain botanical drawing. Good for orientation, never count it as a macro of THIS living specimen.

3 · ROOTED BASE: an actual correctly identified intact fibrous-rooted annual with flowering stems is still needed; in the Hill Country vegetative key the hairy nodes and OPEN rounded sheath margins help, but are not photographed here.

4 · LIGULE: open the inner blade–sheath boundary on a photographed same-specimen leaf. Hill Country key says 1–2 mm truncate erose; FNA says 2–3 mm, WFO 2–3.5 mm of culm leaves. Label leaf position and show both free edge and dorsal hair with a physical 1-mm ruler.

5 · GLUMES: extract two ripe basal glumes, backlight and photograph the one-veined lower and three-veined upper, keeping source specimen, scale and exact observed veins. The 1/3 pattern is NOT unique to Texas brome — do not overcall.
6 · LEMMA: FNA/WFO entire tip versus Kew's bifid two-toothed tip and slightly different awn ranges remain an explicit scientific key hold; image a real matured separated lemma in two orientations.
7 · SPECIES PANELS: 0 target photo; 1 target historical illustration; 2 Japanese; 3 lanceolate; 4 woodland; 5/6 rescuegrass. Don't borrow any different-species photo to 'finish' Texas brome.
8 · MANAGEMENT GATE: unidentified brome remains Bromus sp. pending mature two-glume and lemma review; do not make selective exotic removal calls from a lone drooping awned head.
9 · PUBLICATION: verify actual source CC BY license version, rights-filtered render, all old arrows, and desktop/mobile page. GitHub curation isn't deployment.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: For native versus introduced Bromus, the important structures are glume VEINS, actual lemma dimensions and awns, and an annual or perennial rooted crown—not the word 'brome' or a pretty nodding head.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: 2026-10-26 Lane 5: genuine Cleveland Powell flowering image pixels read from existing GitHub JPEG, historical drawing separately classed; 15 prior broad arrows and licensing retained. No separately documented true root crown, leaf ligule, glume veins, or mature lemma insertion. 1/3 glume vein count is shared with other Bromus; it is a diagnostic combination only with other traits. Three-source ligule length and lemma tip disagreements documented, not silently resolved. New local photographs 0, arrows 0, Pages deployment UNVERIFIED.

what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Whole rooted native-range flowering plant to document annual versus perennial duration and habitat.
Entire mature panicle including every branch origin and 2–3 intact ripe spikelets with 1 cm scale.
Paired lower and upper GLUMES opened without damage: count longitudinal veins using backlight at 10–20× and 1-mm ruler.
Mature lemma with measured length and actual terminal tooth/apex shape plus exact origin and length of single lemma awn.
Cross-section or profile of spikelet to document broad flattened rescuegrass versus more narrow lanceolate type.
Lower leaf sheath HAIRS and true membranous LIGULE at blade–sheath collar, photographed on same plant.
Compare a confirmed Texas brome against local Japanese brome under same 1-mm ruler before invasive removal.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — NATIVE TEXAS BROME, CHECK GLUMES
field_id_short_tiles.short: Real green spikelets and yellow anthers — not a complete rooted plant
field_id_short_tiles.details: Cleveland Powell's source-labelled Texas-brome photo (panel 0) shows several narrow MULTI-FLOWERED spikelets, projecting awnlike tips and emerging yellow anthers. The published 4–7 florets per spikelet have NOT been counted or measured from these unscaled pixels. The original photo crops out the plant base. New Texas source-verified panel 12 shows a flowering shoot growing in rocky soil, and panels 9–11 show attached flowering branches and green spikelets. Actual fibrous roots are still underground and no one image documents a continuous extracted root-to-head specimen. Panel 1 is a historically printed Hitchcock/Chase LINE DRAWING, not a second plant photograph. FNA describes a loose panicle 8–15 cm long and spikelets about 20–30 mm with 4–7 florets, but the photograph has no scale to measure them. For field work, identify complete spikelet units and count individual fertile florets, not all spikelets in the whole head.
field_id_short_tiles.status: NINE GENUINE TEXAS BROME FIELD PHOTOS; FLOWERING SHOOT IN SOIL, REAL SPIKELETS, STILL NO EXPOSED ROOTS

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · ANNUAL ROOTS AND ACTUAL COLLAR
field_id_short_tiles.short: Actual open inside collar photographs now present; ligule 1-mm measurement and fibrous roots pending
field_id_short_tiles.details: The Texas Hill Country VEGETATIVE key (Hagenbuch & Lemke 2015) reports solitary or tufted annual shoots, pubescent nodes, rounded OPEN hairy sheaths, a continuous collar, and a 1–2-mm TRUNCATE EROSE membrane ligule. FNA describes a 2–3-mm lanceolate, pubescent, obtuse/erose ligule; WFO gives culm leaves 2–3(–3.5) mm and dorsal hairs, while Kew calls the margin eciliate. These differ partly by tissue/leaf position and treatment. New genuine Texas photos 7 (outer sheath) and 8 (true culm node) show the exterior. New source-verified New Braunfels panels 13 and 14 show the ACTUAL OPENED INNER blade/sheath junction with a translucent tissue flap consistent with membranous ligule and its side view. Because it may be partly torn and lacks a 1-mm ruler, free-edge identity and length are still not certified. Panel 12 shows the base above rocky soil, but NO exposed fibrous roots. These are real progress on the correct anatomy without pretending the annual root crown is photographed. Next: a source-verified flowering plant with intact fibrous base, one split sheath, blade/sheath INSIDE junction face-on and dorsal membrane beside physical 1-mm ruler. Never label a node or outer sheath hair as a ligule.
field_id_short_tiles.status: REAL OUTER SHEATH, NODE AND INNER COLLAR MEMBRANE PHOTOGRAPHED; FREE LIGULE MM SCALE/ROOTS MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · MEASURE TWO PERSISTENT GLUMES
field_id_short_tiles.short: 1-veined lower / 3-veined upper glumes: critical but NOT unique
field_id_short_tiles.details: Dissect ONE mature source-authenticated Texas-brome spikelet. Remove and backlight the TWO basal OUTER GLUMES — not inner lemma bracts — with a real millimeter ruler. FNA reports lower 6–9 mm/ONE vein, upper 8–10.5 mm/THREE veins; GrassBase lists somewhat shorter lengths but agrees on 1/3 venation. This excludes Japanese brome (often lower 3–5, upper 7) but does not alone prove TEXAS brome: other bromes such as B. tectorum ALSO can have 1/3-veined glumes. Panel 2 Japanese and panel 3 lanceolate are DIFFERENT species. New source-verified real Texas green spikelets in panels 9 and 10 are good for finding the floral bracts but DO NOT individually resolve lower or upper glume veins. The illustration is not photographic proof of 1/3 venation.
field_id_short_tiles.status: CRITICAL REAL BACKLIT SAME-VOUCHER GLUME PAIR NOT PHOTOGRAPHED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · LEMMA TIP AND SUBAPICAL AWN — HOLD CONFLICT
field_id_short_tiles.short: Lemma tip differences held: FNA entire, Kew bifid
field_id_short_tiles.details: FNA/WFO describe an entire acute-to-subulate lemma tip, lemma 9–15 mm and a straight awn 4–8 mm inserted less than 1.5 mm below its apex. Kew GrassBase describes a short two-lobed or bifid apex and 6–10 mm awn. Do NOT blend these as if one photographic character is settled. In the single authentic Texas photo, whole projecting awns are visible but the lemma tip and awn insertion are not resolved; panel 1's ink drawing cannot establish the photographed specimen's apex. The next specimen should have both adaxial/dorsal 10–20× macro of a separated fully mature lemma with its end and original awn, physical 1-mm reference and confirmed voucher.
field_id_short_tiles.status: LITERATURE TIP DISAGREEMENT RETAINED; ANATOMICALLY CERTAIN REAL LEMMA MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · LOOK-ALIKES — JAPANESE, LANCEOLATE, WOODLAND
field_id_short_tiles.short: Compare actual Japanese panel 2, lanceolate panel 3, woodland panel 4
field_id_short_tiles.details: Existing DIFFERENT-species panels: 2 = introduced B. japonicus, 3 = introduced B. lanceolatus, 4 = native perennial B. pubescens, and 5/6 = introduced broad-floreted rescuegrass B. catharticus. Panel 0 is the ONLY photographed B. texensis. Important additional look-alike: B. tectorum (not yet pictured in this gallery) may also have lower 1-veined and upper 3-veined glumes, but generally has longer awns and different leafy growth/sheath characters. The native Texas brome is scarce in regional floras; keep Bromus sp. if an observed plant lacks measured specimen evidence instead of automatically removing it or claiming native Hays presence from a generalized Texas distribution.
field_id_short_tiles.status: IDENTITIES AND LIMITS VERIFIED; NATIVE-VS-INTRODUCED COMPARISON NOT MORPHOLOGICALLY CLOSED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 06 · PUBLIC-READY GATE — TWO LANE HANDOFFS
field_id_short_tiles.short: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — nine real Texas images, key measured glumes and roots still missing
field_id_short_tiles.details: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO: a source-vouchered rooted flowering Texas-brome annual with actual fibrous root crown and hairy lower sheaths, inner true membranous ligule with a physical 1-mm ruler, complete flowering head, mature opened single spikelet showing separately two BACKLIT glumes and actually counted veins, removed fertile lemma tip and subapical awn with mm scale. For hard look-alikes include verified B. tectorum and B. japonicus samples, because 1/3 venation alone is NOT diagnostic of Texas brome. NEEDS_SITE_QA: NINE installed exact-species CC BY Texas photographic JPEGs (one original Cleveland Powell, five additional Cleveland Powell, three Eric Knight New Braunfels), ONE PD historical illustration distinct from a real photo, five other-species comparison panels, original 15 markers kept, exact individual photo rights and displayed credits/mobile arrows, successful Pages deployment. Keep range flags and FNA vs Kew/WFO lemma-tip/ligule disagreements; don't mark 100%.

published_measurements_not_photo_verifie.ligule: Hill Country vegetative key approximately 1–2 mm truncate-erose; FNA approximately 2–3 mm; WFO culm leaf approximately 2–3(–3.5) mm; leaf position and membrane surfaces must be recorded.

grass_species_finalization_20261027.local_lookalikes: Introduced B. japonicus commonly 3–5/7-veined glumes; introduced B. lanceolatus typically larger 25–50-mm many-flowered spikelets; native perennial B. pubescens has hairy lemmas; introduced B. catharticus has broad flattened often short-awned spikelets (comparison only).
